name: Elimination Half-Life from Rate Constant
description: Computes a drug's elimination half-life as the natural log of 2 divided by the elimination rate constant. It is the time for the plasma concentration to fall by half under first-order kinetics.
notes: The result carries the reciprocal of the rate constant's time unit (here hours). Valid only for first-order (linear) elimination; saturable kinetics do not have a constant half-life.

name: Elimination Rate Constant (CL/Vd)
description: Gives the first-order elimination rate constant as clearance divided by the volume of distribution. It sets the fractional rate at which drug is removed from the body per unit time.
notes: Clearance and volume units must be consistent (e.g. L/h and L) so the constant comes out per hour. Assumes a one-compartment model with linear elimination.

name: Total Body Clearance (ke and Vd)
description: Computes total body clearance as the elimination rate constant multiplied by the volume of distribution. It represents the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time.
notes: Result units follow the inputs (here L/h). This is the inverse relationship of ke = CL/Vd and assumes first-order, one-compartment kinetics.

name: Volume of Distribution (Dose/C0)
description: Estimates the apparent volume of distribution after an IV bolus as the dose divided by the initial plasma concentration extrapolated to time zero. It links the dose to the concentration it produces.
notes: C0 is the theoretical concentration at time zero, found by back-extrapolating the elimination phase. Volume is apparent, not a real physiological volume, and can exceed total body water.

name: Apparent Volume of Distribution (CL/ke)
description: Gives the apparent volume of distribution as clearance divided by the elimination rate constant. It is an alternative way to obtain Vd when clearance and ke are known.
notes: Clearance and ke units must be compatible (e.g. L/h and 1/h) so the result is a volume. Assumes linear, one-compartment pharmacokinetics.

name: Loading Dose (with Bioavailability)
description: Calculates the loading dose needed to reach a target plasma concentration as target concentration times volume of distribution, divided by bioavailability. It front-loads the drug to reach therapeutic levels quickly.
notes: Bioavailability F is a fraction between 0 and 1 (use 1 for IV). Concentration and volume units must match so the dose comes out in mass units (mg).

name: Loading Dose (Salt Factor and Bioavailability)
description: Computes the loading dose accounting for the salt factor as target concentration times volume of distribution, divided by the product of salt factor and bioavailability. The salt factor corrects for the active drug fraction in a salt formulation.
notes: The salt factor S is the fraction of the salt that is active drug; both S and F lie between 0 and 1. Match concentration and volume units so the result is a mass dose.

name: Maintenance Dose (Steady-State)
description: Calculates the maintenance dose per interval to sustain a target steady-state concentration as target concentration times clearance times dosing interval, divided by bioavailability. It replaces the drug eliminated each interval.
notes: Clearance and interval time units must be consistent; bioavailability F is a fraction (1 for IV). This gives the dose per dosing interval, not per day unless the interval equals a day.

name: Absolute Bioavailability
description: Determines absolute bioavailability by comparing oral and IV exposure: the oral AUC times the IV dose, divided by the IV AUC times the oral dose. It is the fraction of an oral dose reaching systemic circulation intact.
notes: AUCs should be measured to infinity for the same drug; the two AUC units and the two dose units must each match. Result is a dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1.

name: AUC (IV Bolus, Dose over Clearance)
description: Computes the total area under the plasma concentration-time curve after an IV bolus as the dose divided by clearance. AUC reflects overall systemic drug exposure.
notes: Applies to IV administration with F = 1 and linear kinetics; for other routes divide by CL and multiply by bioavailability. Dose and clearance units set the AUC unit (mg·h/L).

name: AUC by Trapezoidal Rule (Segment)
description: Computes the area under one segment of a concentration-time curve using the trapezoidal rule: the average of the two endpoint concentrations times the time interval between them. Summing segments gives total AUC.
notes: This covers a single interval only; add all segments for full AUC. The linear trapezoidal rule slightly overestimates area during rapidly declining concentrations, where a log-trapezoidal method is preferred.

name: Plasma Concentration (IV Bolus, 1-Compartment)
description: Gives the plasma drug concentration at time t after an IV bolus in a one-compartment model: dose over volume of distribution times e to the power negative ke times t. Concentration decays exponentially from its initial value.
notes: ke and t must use matching time units; at t = 0 the concentration equals dose/Vd. Assumes instantaneous distribution and first-order elimination.

name: Steady-State Concentration (IV Infusion)
description: Computes the steady-state plasma concentration during a constant IV infusion as the infusion rate divided by clearance. At steady state, drug input equals elimination.
notes: Infusion rate and clearance units must be consistent so the result is a concentration (mg/L). This plateau is reached after roughly four to five half-lives of continuous infusion.

name: Plasma Concentration During Infusion
description: Gives the rising plasma concentration at time t during a constant IV infusion as the steady-state level (k0 over CL) times (1 minus e to the power negative ke times t). Concentration approaches steady state asymptotically.
notes: ke and t must share time units; the fraction of steady state reached depends only on ke and t. Valid for one-compartment linear kinetics before the infusion stops.

name: Average Steady-State Concentration
description: Computes the average plasma concentration at steady state during repeated dosing as bioavailability times dose, divided by clearance times the dosing interval. It reflects average exposure over a dosing cycle.
notes: This is the time-averaged concentration, not the peak or trough. Clearance and interval units must match; F is a fraction (1 for IV). Assumes linear pharmacokinetics.

name: Accumulation Factor
description: Gives the drug accumulation factor at steady state for repeated dosing as 1 divided by (1 minus e to the power negative ke times the dosing interval). It quantifies how much concentrations build up compared with a single dose.
notes: ke and interval must use matching time units. Shorter intervals relative to half-life produce larger accumulation; the factor is always greater than 1 and assumes linear kinetics.

name: Steady-State Peak Concentration (Multiple IV Bolus)
description: Computes the peak (post-dose) plasma concentration at steady state for repeated IV bolus dosing as (dose over Vd) divided by (1 minus e to the power negative ke times the interval). It is the single-dose peak multiplied by the accumulation factor.
notes: ke and interval units must match. This gives the maximum concentration just after a dose at steady state; the corresponding trough is found by multiplying by e^(-ke*ti).

name: Steady-State Trough Concentration
description: Gives the trough (pre-dose) plasma concentration at steady state for repeated IV bolus dosing: (dose over Vd) times e to the power negative ke times interval, divided by (1 minus that exponential). It is the minimum concentration just before the next dose.
notes: ke and interval must share time units. This trough equals the steady-state peak multiplied by e^(-ke*ti); assumes one-compartment linear kinetics.

name: Dosing Interval from Peak-to-Trough Ratio
description: Computes the dosing interval needed to decline from a peak to a trough concentration as the natural log of the peak-to-trough ratio divided by the elimination rate constant. It sets the spacing between doses.
notes: Requires Cmax greater than Cmin; the result is in the reciprocal time unit of ke (here hours). Assumes first-order elimination and that decay occurs only between doses.

name: Estimated GFR (Schwartz Bedside)
description: Estimates the glomerular filtration rate in children using the bedside Schwartz equation: an empirical constant times height divided by serum creatinine. It gives a quick kidney-function estimate.
notes: Height is in cm and serum creatinine in mg/dL, using the standardized bedside constant (about 0.413). Intended for pediatric patients; result is normalized to 1.73 m^2 body surface area.

name: Fraction of Drug Remaining
description: Gives the fraction of drug remaining in the body at time t under first-order elimination as e to the power of negative elimination rate constant times time. It ranges from 1 at time zero toward 0.
notes: ke and t must use matching time units; the result is a dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1. Multiply by 100 for a percentage; assumes linear elimination.

name: Fraction Eliminated After n Half-Lives
description: Computes the fraction of drug eliminated after n half-lives as 1 minus 0.5 raised to the power n. After one half-life 50% is gone, after four half-lives about 94%.
notes: n need not be an integer, but assumes first-order kinetics where each half-life removes half the remaining drug. Result is a dimensionless fraction approaching 1.

name: Time to Target Concentration (First-Order)
description: Computes the time for a plasma concentration to decline from an initial value to a target under first-order elimination as the natural log of the initial-to-target ratio divided by the elimination rate constant. Useful for timing when a level is reached.
notes: Requires C0 greater than the target C; result is in the reciprocal time unit of ke (here hours). Applies only to first-order decay with no further dosing.

name: Fraction of Steady State Reached
description: Gives the fraction of the steady-state concentration attained after time t of continuous dosing as 1 minus e to the power negative ke times time. It rises from 0 toward 1 asymptotically.
notes: ke and t must share time units; about 94% of steady state is reached after four half-lives. Assumes constant dosing and first-order elimination.

name: Hepatic Extraction Ratio
description: Computes the hepatic extraction ratio as the difference between arterial and venous drug concentrations divided by the arterial concentration. It is the fraction of drug removed by the liver in a single pass.
notes: Both concentrations must share units; the result is a fraction between 0 and 1. High-extraction drugs (ratio near 1) are sensitive to changes in hepatic blood flow.

name: Hepatic Clearance (Well-Stirred Model)
description: Estimates hepatic clearance using the well-stirred model: hepatic blood flow times the product of unbound fraction and intrinsic clearance, divided by that product plus blood flow. It combines flow and metabolic capacity limits.
notes: Flow Q and intrinsic clearance CLint must share units; fu is a fraction between 0 and 1. Clearance is flow-limited when fu·CLint far exceeds Q, and capacity-limited when it is much smaller.

name: Apparent Oral Clearance
description: Computes the apparent oral clearance as bioavailability times the oral dose divided by the AUC. It reflects clearance relative to the fraction of drug absorbed.
notes: AUC should be measured to infinity for the oral dose; F is a fraction (use 1 if unknown to get CL/F). Dose and AUC units set the clearance unit (L/h).

name: Elimination Half-Life (Vd and Clearance)
description: Computes a drug's elimination half-life from its volume of distribution and clearance as 0.693 (natural log of 2) times Vd divided by clearance. It shows how distribution and clearance jointly set the half-life.
notes: Vd and clearance units must be compatible (e.g. L and L/h) so the result is a time. A larger volume lengthens and a higher clearance shortens the half-life; assumes linear kinetics.

name: Therapeutic Index
description: Computes the therapeutic index as the median toxic dose (TD50) divided by the median effective dose (ED50). A larger value indicates a wider margin between effective and toxic doses.
notes: Both doses must share units so the index is dimensionless. A low therapeutic index means careful dosing and monitoring; the metric does not capture the full dose-response curve overlap.

name: Michaelis-Menten Elimination Rate
description: Gives the drug elimination rate under saturable Michaelis-Menten kinetics as the maximum rate times substrate concentration, divided by the Michaelis constant plus concentration. The rate approaches Vmax at high concentrations.
notes: Km and Cs must share concentration units; when Cs equals Km the rate is half of Vmax. This describes nonlinear elimination, so clearance is not constant across concentrations.

name: Free (Unbound) Drug Concentration
description: Computes the free (unbound) drug concentration as the total plasma concentration times the unbound fraction. Only the free drug is pharmacologically active and available to tissues.
notes: The unbound fraction fu is between 0 and 1; the result shares the total concentration unit. fu can change with protein binding alterations from disease, other drugs, or concentration.

name: Volume of Distribution at Steady State
description: Computes the steady-state volume of distribution using non-compartmental analysis as the IV dose times the area under the moment curve, divided by the square of the AUC. It reflects the true distribution volume independent of elimination.
notes: Applies to IV dosing; AUMC and AUC must be measured to infinity with consistent units (the AUC is squared). Vss is model-independent and generally differs from the terminal-phase Vd.

name: Mean Residence Time
description: Estimates the average time a drug molecule stays in the body by dividing the area under the first-moment concentration-time curve (AUMC) by the area under the concentration-time curve (AUC). It is a non-compartmental measure of drug persistence.
notes: AUMC and AUC must be extrapolated to infinity for a true MRT; truncated data underestimates it. The result reflects intravenous bolus dosing unless corrected for infusion or absorption time.

name: Corrected QT Interval (Bazett)
description: Corrects the measured ECG QT interval for heart rate using Bazett's formula, dividing QT by the square root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT to a heart rate of 60 bpm so intervals can be compared across rates.
notes: QT is in milliseconds but RR must be in seconds. Bazett over-corrects at fast rates and under-corrects at slow rates; Fridericia or other formulas are preferred outside 60-100 bpm.

name: Corrected QT Interval (Fridericia)
description: Corrects the ECG QT interval for heart rate using Fridericia's formula, dividing QT by the cube root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT to 60 bpm and is more reliable than Bazett at extreme heart rates.
notes: QT is in milliseconds and RR in seconds. The cube-root correction reduces rate dependence but still assumes a stable, regular rhythm; irregular rhythms make any single RR unrepresentative.

name: Corrected Serum Calcium (Albumin)
description: Adjusts measured serum calcium for low albumin, adding 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL. It estimates the calcium level that would be seen at a normal albumin, since much calcium is albumin-bound.
notes: Calcium is in mg/dL and albumin in g/dL; the 4 g/dL reference and 0.8 factor are unit-specific. The correction is an approximation and unreliable in critical illness or altered protein binding; ionized calcium is definitive.

name: Calculated Serum Osmolality
description: Estimates serum osmolality from its major osmotically active solutes: twice the sodium (for accompanying anions) plus glucose and blood urea nitrogen converted from mg/dL to mmol/L by dividing by 18 and 2.8. It approximates measured osmolality.
notes: Sodium is in mEq/L, glucose and BUN in mg/dL; the divisors 18 and 2.8 are mg/dL-specific conversions. A large gap between this estimate and measured osmolality suggests unmeasured osmoles such as alcohols.

name: Winter's Formula (Expected pCO2)
description: Predicts the expected arterial pCO2 for adequate respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis, as 1.5 times the bicarbonate plus 8 mmHg. Comparing measured pCO2 to this value detects a superimposed respiratory disorder.
notes: Bicarbonate is in mEq/L and the result in mmHg (typically +/- 2). A measured pCO2 above the predicted range indicates concurrent respiratory acidosis; below it, respiratory alkalosis. Valid only for metabolic acidosis.

name: Bateman Equation (Oral Absorption Plasma Concentration)
description: Computes plasma drug concentration over time after a single oral (extravascular) dose using the Bateman equation, which combines first-order absorption and elimination into a rise-then-fall concentration curve.
notes: Requires ka to differ from ke (the formula is undefined if they are equal). Assumes a one-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination and complete bioavailability.

name: Hill Equation (Emax Model, Dose-Response)
description: Models the drug effect E as a function of concentration C using the Hill (Emax) equation, E = Emax*C^n/(EC50^n+C^n), producing a sigmoid dose-response curve saturating at Emax.
notes: EC50 is the concentration giving half-maximal effect, and the Hill coefficient n controls curve steepness (n=1 gives simple hyperbolic saturation). Assumes a single-site, reversible receptor-binding model.
